blocks.text: Moses forbids the eating of יענה jaana as unclean. This fits the ostrich well: it nests on the ground, alone among birds it never rises from the earth, and it devours without discrimination whatever presents itself; to say nothing of the fact that its flesh and eggs are a very coarse food and hard to digest. The Africans and Arabs, indeed, do not shrink from eating it. And Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo testify that in Ethiopia the Struthophagi regarded ostriches as a delicacy and took their name from this. In Lucian's Dipsades the Garamantes feed on their eggs. In the Persica of Heraclides of Cumae, among the other dishes served to the king of the Persians are στρουθοὶ οἱ Ἀράβιοι [strouthoi hoi Arabioi], Arabian ostriches, as Athenaeus observes in book 4, chapter 9. In Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 13) the ἐπάϊκλα [epaikla], that is, the desserts, of the king of the Indians are κύκνων τε ὠὰ, καὶ τὰ τῶν χερσαίων, στρουθῶν, καὶ χηνῶν [kyknōn te ōa, kai ta tōn chersaiōn, strouthōn, kai chēnōn], the eggs of swans, ostriches and geese. Indeed, among the Roman emperors, Heliogabalus and Firmus had ostriches [II, 822] served to them. For Lampridius says of the former: He served ostriches and camels at dinners several times. Likewise: At a single dinner he served the heads of six hundred ostriches on many tables, so that their brains might be eaten. And further on: He also had this custom of having dinners served to him such that on one day he would eat only pheasants, [col. 226] and would compose all the courses of pheasant meat alone; likewise on another day of chickens, on another of this or that fish, on another of pork, on another of ostriches. And Vopiscus says of Firmus: He ate much meat; he is said to have eaten an ostrich in a day. But both had grown accustomed to this food in Syria: for Heliogabalus was born at Emesa, Firmus at Seleucia. The physicians, whose business it is to judge the εὐχυμίᾳ [euchymia] or κακοχυμίᾳ [kakochymia] of foods, hardly approve of eating ostriches, as the following passages will make plain. Galen, in chapter 6 of On the Good and Bad Juices of Foods: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς μεγάλοις στρουθοῖς ἅπαντα τὰ μέρη σκληρὰ, καὶ δύσπεπτα, καὶ περιττωματικά· [En de tois megalois strouthois hapanta ta merē sklēra, kai dyspepta, kai perittōmatika] In ostriches all parts are hard, difficult to digest, and productive of excrement. And in book 3, chapter 20 of On the Properties of Foods, where he treats of ostriches and geese: Περιττωματικὴ τοίνυν ἡ σὰρξ αὐτῶν ἐστι, καὶ πολὺ δυσπεπτοτέρα τῆς τῶν προειρημένων πτηνῶν ζώων· [Perittōmatikē toinyn hē sarx autōn esti, kai poly dyspeptotera tēs tōn proeirēmenōn ptēnōn zōōn] Their flesh, therefore, is productive of excrement, and much harder to digest than that of the birds mentioned before. And on eggs, in chapter 22: Ἀμείνω τά τε ἀλεκτορίδων ἐστι, καὶ τὰ τῶν Φασιάνων· Φαυλοτέρα δὲ τὰ τῶν χηνῶν τε, καὶ στρουθοκαμήλων· [Ameinō ta te alektoridōn esti, kai ta tōn Phasianōn; Phaulotera de ta tōn chēnōn te, kai strouthokamēlōn] Best are those of hens and pheasants; worst those of geese and ostriches. Aetius copied these from Galen in the Tetrabiblos, book 1, discourse 2, ch. 131 and 134. And Symeon Seth, to condemn the eating of goose flesh as strongly as possible, says ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ τάξει τεθεῖναι παρὰ τῶν παλαιῶν τῇ τῶν στρουθοκαμήλων σαρκὶ [en tē autē taxei tetheinai para tōn palaiōn tē tōn strouthokamēlōn sarki], that the ancients placed it in the same rank as ostrich flesh. But in the judgement of Rhazes goose flesh is far superior and corrects the κακοχυμίαν [kakochymian] of ostrich flesh. His words are: لحوم النعام غليظة جدا فينبغي ان يصلح باصلاح لحم البط [luḥūm al-naʿām ghalīẓa jiddan fa-yanbaghī an yuṣlaḥ bi-iṣlāḥ laḥm al-baṭṭ] The flesh of ostriches is very coarse, and it must be corrected by joining goose flesh to it. Avicenna, too, says of the ostrich: لحمه غليظ لا ينهضم [laḥmuhu ghalīẓ lā yanhaḍim] Its flesh is coarse and is not digested. And Leo Africanus, in book 6, in the chapter on Dara, asserts that ostrich flesh is very hard and very foul-smelling, and also viscous about the thighs. And Aben-Ezra on Exod. XXIII, 29., anxiously asking why the Law forbids not יענה jaana, that is, the ostrich, in general, but בת יענה bath-jaana, the daughter of the ostrich, as he at any rate interprets it, answers the question thus: דע כי בשר היענה יבש כעץ ואין המנהג שיאכלנו אדם כי אין בו לוחה ולא יאכל מכל המין רק הבת כי היא נקבה וקטנה יש בה מעט לוחה ולא כן הזכר הקטן, Know that the flesh of the ostrich is dry as wood, so that it is not usually eaten, because there is no moisture in it. Therefore of the whole species nothing is eaten except the daughter, which, being female, has some moisture while it is small; but the male does not [II, 823] likewise, even when it is small. I cannot refrain from adding Scaliger's conjecture on Ausonius' verse,
Cook you the egg of the sea-sparrow,

in the eleventh Epistle, to Paulus. He seems, he says, to proclaim a famine for Paulus, staying on his estate Crebennus, when he bids him cook the egg of the sea-sparrow, that is, of the ostrich. For what sweetness is there in an ostrich egg, and a stale one at that? So he wittily says that he goes hungry at the villa of Crebennus, where he had nothing but an ostrich egg.
